lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate
teaching: A **single neuron** multiplies its inputs by weights and adds the products into one number. A **neural network** combines these operations into layers, turning one input vector into a decision vector.

An **LLM** processes fifteen vectors through successive layers and predicts a sixteenth vector, a probability distribution over the next token. An **agentic system** joins whole LLMs into a graph that outlines, writes, criticizes, revises and finalizes the response.
The critic and reviser form a loop so a revised draft can be evaluated again. The agents communicate in English and can work in other human languages and computer languages.
**Inference uses inner products**, while learning uses **SGD and dynamic programming**. Inference processes current inputs with learned weights, while learning changes the weights to reduce error.

**A network makes one static decision, while language flows in time.** In “The wolves that run around Catalina Island ___,” the verb is “are,” because it agrees with “wolves” however far away that word is. In an agentic system, one LLM outlines, one drafts, one criticizes and one writes the final answer. Hallucination dropped enormously once LLMs checked each other.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers
teaching: **Predicting the next word is difficult**, so an LLM uses many layers to develop its input representations. Each layer transforms the vectors produced by the preceding layer.

Within a layer, **heads work in parallel as different experts**. Their contributions are combined into new representations, and the next layer repeats the process with those representations. Heads contribute within one stage, while layers provide successive stages.

**Each head is its own neural network, and each layer has its own heads.** A student who gives advice in one class is a head, and the next class is the next layer. Combining the advice gives a better representation of each vector.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth
teaching: A **dynamical system** applies a rule to its state and feeds the resulting state back in. In the oscillator, position is updated using the old velocity, then velocity is updated using that new position. Repeating the rule produces oscillation.

In **Jordan’s recurrent network**, plan and state units feed a hidden layer, output returns to state units, and self-connections preserve a fading trace. The weights are reused over time, so recent outputs affect the next output.

An **LLM** transforms vectors through successive layers, so depth plays the role of time. Following one number through the layers gives a changing curve. Each layer has its own weights, unlike the same rule reused across time in the oscillator and recurrent network.
The small stock-return graph traces Small, Medium and Large series fluctuating over the same period, another example of quantities changing over time.
**An LLM is a dynamical system like the oscillator.** In the oscillator, x gives the next v and v gives the next x. An LLM does this with tens of thousands of numbers, many times over.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences
teaching: An **LLM** receives fifteen vectors and predicts the following one. The vectors can represent words in a sentence, frames of a spectrogram, patches of a picture, or amino acids in the **insulin B chain**.

The picture is divided into sixteen patches, with fifteen given and the bottom-right patch left to predict. In the protein example the next residue is Y. The original materials differ, but all are represented as **sequences of vectors**.

**The same design was reused by changing what the vectors stand for.** They can be words, pieces of a spectrogram, patches of an image or the amino acids of a protein. One technology solving all of these supports the **horizontal** view, in which every skill uses the same computations.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: One-syllable words like Don, mat and fish follow a **consonant, vowel, consonant** pattern. Clusters are allowed **before and after the vowel** only in certain orders, so split, flat, desk and help are words while *sblit, *lfat, *desb and *hepl are impossible, with the order mirroring around the vowel.

A **long word is a chain of syllables**, each obeying the same rules. t·l is fine across a break in At·lan·tic, but **tl cannot start a syllable**, so *tlantic is impossible, and ng can end a syllable but never start one.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: Guessing the **next letter** of a word start shows **phonotactic knowledge**. After a vowel, as in **ra_**, almost anything can follow. At the start of a word the choices narrow, to **l, r or a vowel** after sp_, b_ and f_, and to **only a vowel** after skr_ and m_.

Each item also has an impossible continuation, such as *spn, *kt, *skrl or *mb. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆**, so a **GPT** trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, with a broad distribution after ra_ and a sharply peaked one after skr_.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables
What an LLM learns
teaching: An LLM learns by guessing a **hidden word**. In “The chef cracks the,” each earlier word gives a clue about the last word, and these links are **interdependencies**. The model spreads its bets over “egg,” “nut” and “code,” with the largest bet on “egg.”
**Learning is nudging the weights** so the right word gets a bigger bet next time. The same idea holds when the signal contains words, sounds and images.
**Guessing the next word is the GPT task.** The weights are nudged by backpropagation so the guesses improve. Multimodal systems are about two to three years old, and people are multimodal too.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms
teaching: Text is **already a row of pieces**, so each piece can become a vector. Speech is **air pressure changing in time**, and an image is **a grid of light**. Neither one contains words.
An LLM can only read a row of vectors. Speech and images therefore have to be **converted into rows of vectors** before the model can read them with text.

**The words, the speech signal and the image can be three versions of one message.** The speech signal is the pressure variation in front of the mouth. Before multimodal systems, text, speech and vision models were each trained separately.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors
teaching: Speech is cut into short slices called **frames**, each about 20 milliseconds long. A **speech encoder**, a network trained on a large amount of audio, turns each slice into a vector.
One second of speech becomes **50 vectors in time order**. The speech is then a row, just like a sentence.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors
teaching: An image is cut into small squares called **patches**. The 16 patches of the egg image are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence.
A **vision encoder** gives one vector per patch. Real systems use patches of 14 to 16 pixels, so one image gives hundreds of vectors.

sections.title: One row with three senses
teaching: Image patches, speech frames and words go into **one row**, with the last word hidden. The earlier words still give clues about the hidden word.
A patch containing an egg and the sound of cracking also help. These links between senses are **cross-modal dependencies**. The game is the same, and some clues now come from other senses.

**The game inside one modality can be played across modalities, because the technology is the same.** The W’s are then about how image patches, speech frames and words relate to one another. After enough training, the W’s are truly multimodal.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words
teaching: “Three cute puppies” is given as an image cut into **18 patches**, as a **spectrogram** of the spoken phrase, and as three written words. In the spectrogram, time runs left to right, higher means higher frequency and darker means more energy.
These are **three views of one event**. Training puts all three into one row and hides one piece for the model to guess.

**The example is an ordinary social media post.** It has an image, a caption and a video with the same words spoken. The W’s come from data like this, which is why paying people for their data is being argued.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word
teaching: The row holds the image, the sound and the words “three cute,” and the last word is hidden. With the words alone, the bets are spread over “kittens,” “puppies” and “babies.”
With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on **“puppies.”** The model bet 0.85 on the true word, so the error is small and **the nudge to the weights is small**.
**The first way gives the system a few words, all the speech and all the patches.** It has to predict the next text word. Its W’s change so that it predicts that word better.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame
teaching: The hidden piece is a **sound frame**, and the row holds the image, the words and the sound heard so far. The earlier frames help because the voice and the formants change smoothly. The words say the next sound is the vowel in “pup,” and the image backs up the words.
A frame is a column of numbers giving the energy in each frequency band. The guess is close but not exact, and **the error nudges the weights**.
**The second way gives the system the patches, the words and half of the speech.** It has to predict the next bit of speech. It uses the speech frames, the words and the patches together.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch
teaching: The hidden piece is an **image patch**, and the row holds the words, the sound and the patches drawn so far. The earlier patches give background and two puppies. “Three” says one more puppy must appear, and “puppies” says to expect dog ears.
The guess is a blurry ear in the average colour of the first two puppies, while the true puppy is dark. **The biggest error is the colour**, because no clue said the third puppy is dark.

**The third way asks for the next patch, which is the third dog.** Two dogs alone could be followed by a kennel or a person. The words and the speech both say “three puppies,” so a third puppy has the highest probability.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one
teaching: A hidden word, a hidden frame or a hidden patch each receives clues from the words, the sound and the image. For a hidden word, “three cute” calls for a plural noun, the word was just spoken, and the image contains puppies.
A clue from **the same sense** says how the signal continues. Clues from **the other senses** say what the thing is. Each sense fills gaps the others leave.

**One post trains the system in every direction.** It goes from speech and vision to text, from text and vision to speech, and so on. **W’s are knowledge**, and here the knowledge is about the bond between speaking, hearing and seeing.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new
teaching: To speak, sound is compressed into **discrete codes** that work like new words in the vocabulary. The model predicts the next code like the next word, and a **decoder** turns the codes back into sound.

Three things are new, which are a shared currency of vectors in one row, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was already learned. What stays the same is **finding the dependencies in the signal**.

**A modality is like a sense, and language counts as one.** Separate LLMs for language, speech, vision and biology have been combined over the last three or four years. Biomedical multimodal LLMs combine scans, notes, lab results and sequences. An ordinary chat system already knows about a hundred languages.
